claims.text: The dominant tribocorrosion mechanism in high-entropy alloys is cyclic formation and mechanical disruption of a protective passive oxide film.
Under static conditions, the alloy forms a robust oxide layer that inhibits corrosion.
Sliding repeatedly removes the passive film and exposes fresh, reactive substrate.
Exposure of the substrate accelerates corrosion and wear.
Rapid film removal combined with delayed repassivation produces total degradation exceeding the sum of wear-only and corrosion-only degradation.
The initial alloy is equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi.
The initial CoCrFeMnNi alloy has a homogeneous, single-phase microstructure.
CoCrFeMnNi naturally forms a stable passive oxide film under ambient conditions.
Matched sliding tests in a dry or inert medium and static immersion tests can separate wear-only and corrosion-only contributions from tribocorrosion.
The passive oxide film is the key structural mediator controlling coupled mechanical and chemical degradation.
Repassivation of the mechanically disrupted film is imperfect under dynamic sliding conditions.
Corrosion-induced surface degradation diminishes the alloy's wear resistance.
Wear-enhanced corrosion and corrosion-enhanced wear form a reinforcing feedback loop.
Tribocorrosion will produce greater mass loss, deeper or wider wear tracks, and higher pit density than the individual wear-only and corrosion-only baselines.
The proposed synergy should hold for high-entropy alloys that form stable passive oxide films.
The prediction may fail for alloys lacking effective passive films.
The prediction may fail when wear is insufficient to disrupt the passive film.
Stabilizing the passive film with a passivation inhibitor should measurably reduce synergistic degradation.
